analysis: Palula puuríi has an accented modern verbal ending, while the inherited long root is unaccented in this citation. The older Shina infinitive pŭróiki likewise includes a new infinitival formation. Neither can directly test preservation of the old finite accent; the causative root pūr- is independently supported and must be compared in equivalent imperative or finite cells.
unresolved: Recover paradigm accents and distinguish the causative from passive 8342.

analysis: Palula puunǰí ‘full’ continues a different stem formation from transitive puuríi ‘fill’. The final short accented i and medial nǰ require an account of the passive/result-state morphology. Because the old entry explicitly supplies both pūryátē and pū́ryatē, this family does not have a unique inherited finite accent even before considering modern derivation.
unresolved: Inspect the modern grammatical category and segmental history of nǰ; do not choose an old accent variant solely from the outcome.

analysis: Gilgit piṭo and Sauji priš reflect different treatment of the old cluster and final nominal material. The Gilgit root is short and the source citation lacks an explicit accent, so the retained o is useful morphological evidence but not a measured early or late contour. Sauji's old transcription supplies no comparable mora information.
unresolved: Recover Gilgit accent from the entry or inflections; check whether piṭo's omission is an editorial or source property.

input: pṓta and independently reconstructed *phōta within a variant-rich family
analysis: Palula phoó is late-accented despite the broad headword's early accent. Its son/boy paradigm and the related feminine phoyī are essential: final-vowel loss and contraction may have redistributed the accent. An account through earlier *pháa and raising is proposed in the grammar, but the old family already contains ō, so the modern vowel quality alone cannot establish that route. The proposed Dravidian connection and substantial old variants further limit a unique input.
unresolved: Read the full boy paradigm and compare Kalkoti púu with the same formation; distinguish a demonstrated relative chronology from a unique reconstruction.

analysis: Palula púutru and all four Schmidt Shina dialects póoc̣o preserve early root prominence with a surviving final gender vowel. Sanskrit au is one long nucleus, so its accent must not be misread as accent on a second syllable. The Palula tr versus Shina retroflex affricate provides an independent segmental correspondence. Kalkoti pootr lacks usable tone in the HKAT source.
unresolved: Determine whether the modern ending requires the attested extension or continues older nominal material; acquire a tone-marked Kalkoti token.

analysis: Gilgit c̣iín has late accent on a long vowel, but its old input has three nuclei and accent on ya. Both pr-to-c̣ and substantial contraction intervene, so the result is not an instance of simple loss of final a from an old long-root oxytone. The DB's *priṅg is a reconstruction embedded in comparative discussion, not an independently attested Shina word.
unresolved: Establish the contracted intermediate and exclude reconstructed comparative fragments from the attested record count.

input: plúṣi and multiple independently reconstructed variants including *priṣu
analysis: Palula príiṇṣu and Guresi/Astori príij̣o/príiẓu share early long-root accent and an unaccented final vowel. This is compatible with old initial prominence but the modern i and retained pr require the variant history, not mechanical derivation from plúṣi. Turner's addendum explicitly discusses the anomalous retention of pr in Shina, where inherited pr normally becomes c̣. Sauji preṣuko has additional derivational material and no reliable mora marking.
unresolved: Check the full addendum for the proposed borrowing route; do not count an expressive or borrowed common form as independent proof of an accent law.

analysis: Palula phalúuṛu is a grain or unit of a round object and can count people colloquially. Its accented long u belongs to additional stem material absent from phála. Final-root accent in the extended modern nominal is therefore the relevant comparison; the shift from the old first syllable is not unexplained phonetic attraction to an inherited ū. The old short-a plural or grain forms are separate cells.
unresolved: Identify the unit suffix's independent productivity and inflection rather than reconstructing its accent from this one word.

input: phálati and independently attested transitive phālayati
analysis: Palula phaalíi ‘tear, split’ and Strand phāl- match the transitive long-root formation better than the broad intransitive headword phálati. The late-accented verbal ending in the dictionary citation is modern morphology; an unaccented bare stem does not contradict it. Selecting the causative is supported by both valency and old root quantity, independently of modern accent.
unresolved: Compare equivalent finite or imperative cells to determine root prominence.

analysis: Ashret phóol, Biori pháal and Gilgit pháal agree on early accent on the old long root. The Ashret/Biori vowel correspondence gives independent evidence for early-accented ā raising in Ashret. Initial aspiration does not force late accent when the vowel was already long, distinguishing this class from later lengthening of old short a in aspirated closed monosyllables. Sauji phal supplies cognacy but no comparable contour.
unresolved: Check inflected cells as a control on fixed versus mobile noun accent.

analysis: Strand phʹîṇ ‘foam’ has early accent, whereas Liljegren phiíṇ ‘steam, vapour’ is late. Both have the raised vowel expected from an earlier early-accented ē stage, so the late modern form may involve subsequent reaccentuation or a semantic/lexical split. The two senses are related but must not be silently merged into one contradictory token or resolved by averaging sources.
unresolved: Inspect each paradigm and speaker/dialect information to distinguish lexical split, variation and transcription disagreement.

analysis: Gilgit bádo ‘prisoner, slave, exile’ is early-accented and retains the nominal ending o. The independently attested Sanskrit báddhaka has both the matching captive sense and a retracted accent. This is a strong case where the broad family's oxytone headword would manufacture an exception. The older Shina badu ‘froze’ belongs to a participial verb cell and should not determine the prisoner's accent class.
unresolved: Document the nominal inflection and keep the frozen participle separately aligned with 9134.

analysis: Gilgit baǰ- ‘freeze’ supplies no vowel accent in its bound-stem citation, and the older infinitive bažóiki accents newer material. The old passive formation supplies a plausible route for dhy to the modern palatal consonant and for the semantic development ‘be bound’ to ‘freeze’. It must be compared with its own inflections and participle, not the nominal bádo ‘prisoner’.
unresolved: Recover present, imperative and perfective accents; avoid double-counting 9126 as a second independent verb.

analysis: Gilgit ban ‘joint’ has a short monosyllabic nucleus with no two-mora contrast. The compound ban b- ‘be closed’ adds a light verb and must not be parsed as a single noun outcome. Palula bandi and Kohistani bandī́ retain additional feminine or oblique material; their final accent is not directly comparable to the bare joint noun. Cluster reduction alone has not produced an obligatory long vowel here.
unresolved: Establish the case/derivation of bandi and retain the short noun as a negative control for universal compensatory lengthening.

analysis: Palula bakáara ‘flock of sheep and goats’ has second-syllable early long-vowel accent, whereas the old simplex is initially accented. The collective meaning and changed stem formation require analysis before labeling this a sound-law exception. Its ā is not an inherited long vowel of bárkara, so an attraction rule conditioned by old quantity would be circular here. Loss or dissimilation of r also needs explicit accounting.
unresolved: Inspect the collective suffix and compare singular goat formations; determine whether lengthening follows the new accent.

analysis: Gilgit and Kohistani baál ‘child’ show late accent on the preserved old long root after loss of final accented a. Independent Gilgit sources agree. This is a clean counterpart to early long-root barytones and does not require postulating newly created vowel length or a surviving accent-bearing suffix. The wider family's bālaka and feminine forms should remain separate formations.
unresolved: Confirm mobility in the noun paradigm and add cognates in languages where the concept is lexically replaced.

analysis: Palula baaugáaṛu ‘shoulder’ is a compound whose accented second constituent cannot test retention of bāhú's accent. Gilgit bóo~i ‘sleeve’ is a contracted feminine or relational formation, while ba-khúni ‘elbow’ is another compound. Shared arm semantics support the family but do not establish identical accentual inputs for shoulder, sleeve and elbow.
unresolved: Analyze each second constituent and sleeve inflection; flag the unequal-vowel sequence in baau for manual syllabification.

analysis: Palula bhíia and Biori bhíie have early prominence on the long root in the imperative-style citation. The old finite form contains reduplication and an accented ē grade, so a direct word-position comparison would be misleading. Root accent is compatible, but the two adjacent unequal vowels in the modern form require source-based syllabification and an explicit paradigm rather than an automatic nucleus count.
unresolved: Recover the modern fear verb's stem classes and contraction history.

analysis: Palula and all four Schmidt Shina dialects bíi retain early accent on the inherited long root after intervocalic j and final a disappear. This provides a particularly clean early-accent control because old ī does not undergo the ā-to-oo raising that complicates many western examples. Hultman's Kalkoti bii is explicitly toneless, a meaningful contrast requiring a separate tonal analysis rather than treating its missing acute as missing data.
unresolved: Link and verify the Kalkoti record with its source-specific tone status, and inspect noun mobility.

analysis: Palula búǰa ‘understand’ and bhuuǰóo ‘wake someone’ differ in aspiration, quantity, valency and conjugational formation. The accented causative ending in the latter is independently motivated by transitivity, while the understanding verb's short root is initially prominent in its imperative citation. These are not two competing direct accent reflexes of one unmodified finite word.
unresolved: Trace the aspiration and causative formation through full paradigms; keep the lexical senses separate.

analysis: Buddruss's Gilgit bat ‘rice dish’ is short, despite old kt reduction. A late long-vowel outcome cannot be inferred from the old oxytone accent when the modern vowel is not long. Older Palula bhāt versus bat already indicate quantity/source differences. This family is a necessary control on the proposed Gilgit late-lengthening cluster class, not evidence that every reduced cluster lengthens.
unresolved: Recover tone-marked Palula and Kohistani/Astori comparisons and verify whether particular cluster types or paradigms condition quantity.

analysis: Strand bhʹâru ‘load’ has early accent on long a, while the independently attested old bhára has a short root vowel. Extension plus later lengthening offers a possible source of Palula bháaru that does not require unexplained failure of early old ā to raise. This must be evaluated jointly with family 9459 bhārá, under which another source places the same modern load word.
unresolved: The short base is attested, but the particular extended intermediate remains a hypothesis; establish its morphological and dialectal support before preferring it.

analysis: Palula hínu, Gilgit han and Kalkoti in are grammaticalized present copula forms, whereas older Shina boiki/bōnu belongs to ‘become’. Their divergent material and inflectional histories make a direct comparison with the accent of bhávati inappropriate. A short unaccented copula citation is especially sensitive to clitic and sentential prosody, not just inherited lexical accent.
unresolved: Separate copular cells from lexical become and examine their actual stress behavior in the grammars.

input: bhārá; compare independently attested bhára in 9393
analysis: Gilgit baár fits the old long-root oxytone class directly. Palula bháaru has an unaccented ending and early root prominence, but its unraised aa is unexpected if it directly continued early-retracted old ā. The same word is linked by Strand to short-root bhára, which could acquire new length after extension and after the old raising change. This alternative is motivated by segmental chronology and an attested base, not merely by the desired accent.
unresolved: Test both inputs against morphology and Biori/Sauji evidence; retain the proposed short-base derivation as tentative rather than a database correction.

analysis: Gilgit baáo ‘object, vessel’ preserves late prominence on the old long-root material while v weakens or disappears. Because a following o remains, this is not literally the same surface template as baál or baár. The result can support retraction of old final accent into the root, but the unequal-vowel sequence must be parsed from the source before assigning a syllable count or a simple monosyllabic class.
unresolved: Inspect singular/oblique forms and distinguish hiatus from a single complex nucleus.

analysis: Gilgit bičh- ‘request, ask for’ is an unaccented bound stem with a short vowel. The old cluster gives a plausible source for the affricate/aspiration, but neither the old finite ending nor an equivalent modern finite accent is present in the citation. It cannot count as an observed early or late reflex merely because the old word was barytone.
unresolved: Recover finite and imperative forms from the glossary's conjugational material.

analysis: Strand bh- explicitly represents a past/nonfinite stem and has no vowel on which to observe accent. The older Shina bulu is unmarked and belongs to a fuller participial formation. The old long-root oxytone input is therefore known, but no comparable modern contour is supplied by the linked citations.
unresolved: Align full past forms in the become paradigm and keep them distinct from the present copula under 9416.

analysis: Gilgit/Kohistani/Guresi búṭo/búṭa/búṭɨ have a short initially accented root after contraction and shortening. Strand buṭhʹe ‘all’ instead marks the final vowel; it may represent a different quantifier or inflectional cell. The old first-syllable prominence is compatible with Shina, but the major syllable loss and lexicalization prevent a simple long-vowel correspondence claim.
unresolved: Determine the Palula quantifier's number/case and the relation of its final e to Shina gender endings.

analysis: Strand bhrimboṛʹî ‘wasp’ has final ī prominence, whereas an older Palula transcription brhimbṓṛi ‘bee, wasp’ marks the preceding vowel. The stem has expressive consonantal and vocalic changes and an added feminine formation. This is a real source/cell discrepancy; the old final-a accent does not uniquely predict which modern suffix or stem syllable should carry it.
unresolved: Check the older transcription, source dialect and feminine paradigm; distinguish wasp from bee lexical senses.

analysis: Palula bhróo/Biori bhrúu and Shina ẓáa/j̣áa show early root accent, compatible with old long-root barytonesis despite strong segmental divergence. Published Palula bhroó variants elsewhere require separate recording, and Sauji brāū́ ‘my brother’ is a possessive form rather than a bare lexical duplicate. Kalkoti dra is tone-unmarked in HKAT and cannot establish a loss of accent.
unresolved: Reconcile source-specific brother paradigms and verify early/late variants without selecting only the agreeing citations.

analysis: Gilgit machíi ‘fly’ has final early-long ī accent, unlike the initial accent of both mákṣā and the attested feminine mákṣikā. A derivational account cannot simply label -ikā as historically suffix-accented: the old accent is explicitly initial. Later feminine-class reaccentuation or a different intermediary remains necessary. Compare honey 9989, whose superficially similar modern shape has a different old derivational history.
unresolved: Recover inflection and the formation's intermediate vowel quantity; preserve this as a genuine reaccentuation problem.

input: máṇḍala and *manda among the recorded alternatives
analysis: Gilgit múuni ‘lap’ is early-accented, while older mano ‘hip’ and muñi ‘lap’ suggest different gender and stem formations. The reduction from a three-syllable disc/circle word is substantial, and Turner independently allows a shorter *manda variant. Shared body-region semantics support comparison but do not isolate which formation or accent the modern feminine inherited.
unresolved: Read the complete etymological discussion and the lap paradigm; do not transfer máṇḍala's accent automatically to an unaccented reconstructed short input.

analysis: Gilgit manúuko straightforwardly preserves early prominence on inherited ū. Palula maṭróok has a different tr-bearing stem assigned to the independently reconstructed *maṭrakka family, so its long oo cannot be treated as the same inherited vowel without further argument. Sauji miṇḍā́ka has still another vowel. Turner explicitly attributes the variant-rich frog names to expressive/taboo processes; that is evidence for unstable segmental forms, not a license to assign arbitrary accents.
unresolved: Reconstruct the Palula vowel chronology and distinguish attested old quantity from inferred intermediates.

analysis: Palula mheél ‘buttermilk’ has late long-vowel accent, while Gilgit mel is short. Both involve substantial contraction and aspiration relocation from the old participle. The late Palula vowel is compatible with accent left by lost final material, but it is newly created rather than a preserved old long root. This family therefore tests contraction chronology separately from the clean kālá/baál class.
unresolved: Establish intermediate forms and explain western length versus Gilgit short quantity using source paradigms.

analysis: Palula mhoóru has late prominence on its long root before an unaccented u; older mohóro retains evidence for the contracted medial syllable. Its root-final accent locus is compatible with the extended adjective pattern, but its late mora is not the early mora of tíiṇu or puróoṇu. Contraction of multiple old syllables and aspiration relocation provide independent conditioning to test rather than forcing all u-final adjectives into one contour class.
unresolved: Determine the contraction sequence and whether its late alignment is shared by other VhV-derived long vowels.

input: mádhya with independently attested madhyam, mádhyēna, madhyāt and madhyē
analysis: Palula méeǰi has early root prominence, whereas Gilgit maǰaá is finally late-accented. These relational words can descend from different old case forms, independently listed in the entry, so a common noun-headword accent does not provide a unique postpositional input. The Palula front vowel also implicates the retained i formation; Gilgit's final aa requires its own case or extension history.
unresolved: Match modern syntactic construction and case government to candidate older forms rather than selecting an input by accent alone.

analysis: Strand man- ‘say’ is a short bound stem without explicit accent. The semantic path from think to say is plausible, but Palula dictionary forms elsewhere are assigned to mantráyatē 9837. These are competing analyses of essentially the same modern speech verb, not independent evidence for two sound correspondences.
unresolved: Compare segmental expectations for loss of tr and the full speech paradigm; retain both etymologies until independently discriminated.

analysis: Gilgit manúẓo is accented on the final root syllable before the gender ending o, unlike old initial mánuṣa. Because both root syllables remain short, this is a clear accent-locus shift that cannot be attributed to attraction to an inherited long vowel. It is a strong member of the morphologically extended nominal class, subject to independent confirmation of the ending and paradigm.
unresolved: Read the inflection and document whether an old extended formation or later analogical class membership best explains the ending.

analysis: Gilgit mor ‘word, matter’ is a short monosyllable, while móẓiye displays initial accent in a fuller form with a different consonant reflex. The expanded form may expose the original accent obscured by monosyllabicity, but its grammatical cell must be read before treating the pair as free variants. Old ntr simplification and consonant alternation make the paradigm particularly informative.
unresolved: Identify the exact cell of móẓiye and determine whether root accent remains fixed throughout the paradigm.

analysis: Palula maníi ‘say, call, recite’ accents a modern verbal ending and has lost the old tr material if this etymology is correct. Strand instead links the short man- root to manutḗ. The two proposals cannot be counted as separate lexical outcomes, and modern final accent by itself does not decide the competing segmental derivations.
unresolved: Evaluate the old semantic and consonantal evidence, then align identical modern verb cells.

analysis: Gilgit madúr ‘horse stable’ preserves two short nuclei with prominence on the last surviving syllable after the old accented final ā is lost. This is compatible with accent docking leftward at apocope, without yielding an early/late long-vowel contrast. It extends the inquiry beyond monosyllables: old final prominence can leave a detectable position on a preceding short syllable.
unresolved: Check the oblique paradigm and whether the final ā was a productive feminine ending at the relevant historical stage.

analysis: Gilgit moón ‘jealousy’ has late accent on a newly long vowel after contraction of the old nyu sequence. The old word was finally accented but did not have a long first vowel, so this belongs with contraction-created length rather than inherited-long-root apocope. The semantic narrowing from anger/passion to jealousy does not itself require a new morphological formation.
unresolved: Reconstruct the vowel and glide sequence and check the nominal paradigm for mobility.

input: máratē and the broader mar-/mr̥- paradigm
analysis: Palula máara/Biori máare and Strand mʹâr- have early root prominence with long a in the imperative citation. Turner explicitly discusses inheritance of mar- versus expansion from other verbal cells, so the modern root need not derive from an arbitrarily selected finite form. Kalkoti märuun is a present and Kundal Shahi mɛrgo a past; their accent and quantity cannot be compared as identical forms.
unresolved: Use aligned verbal cells and determine which length is phonological versus imperative-specific.

analysis: Palula máakaṛ shifts prominence from the old second syllable to the first while losing the first r and lengthening the initial vowel. This is a genuine residual for simple accent retention, since two modern root syllables remain. The old entry suggests extension of marka, but its accent is not supplied; that proposal cannot automatically solve the modern initial accent. Quantity and accent may be jointly affected by the cluster history.
unresolved: Compare regional monkey cognates and the source paradigm; test a independently motivated retraction/lengthening chronology.

analysis: Strand mʹîš ‘man’ has early long-vowel accent compatible with the old initial prominence after rty contraction and vowel change. Kundal Shahi mɛ̄̃c is a useful segmental comparison but its legacy notation does not directly establish mora alignment. This family must be cross-checked against alternative mánuṣya links for similar modern man words and Kalkoti meéš, which has late H.
unresolved: Discriminate the human-word etymologies using consonant correspondences and link the Kalkoti token without assuming identical tone history.

analysis: Palula máaṇḍa is initially early-accented with a nasal cluster; Turner explicitly notes that mard- and *mr̥nd- have converged in several languages. The nasal cannot simply be ignored when assigning an input. Initial root prominence is compatible with the broad finite headword, but the specific nasal input lacks independently recorded accent and the modern citation is an imperative cell.
unresolved: Determine which stem formation accounts for the nasal and compare the full knead paradigm.

analysis: Palula bráam and Strand brʹâmu preserve early prominence on material from the old first syllable after metathesis and strengthening of a nasal to b. Their new long a cannot be treated as an inherited ā; the short old root and modern consonant rearrangement provide an independent chronology problem. The final u difference may reflect source or inflectional formation rather than a separate accent class.
unresolved: Check the segmental intermediate and nominal paradigm, including whether the final u is a citation variant.

input: māṁsá, with mā́s independently recorded in the old family
analysis: Palula mhaás and Gilgit/Kohistani/Guresi moós consistently have late accent on the old long root after loss of final accented a. Secondary aspiration and nasal developments differ across branches while the contour agrees. This provides a clean late-accent comparison against early-accented mā́sa ‘month’; the independently recorded contracted old mā́s must remain an alternative formation rather than silently replace the principal input.
unresolved: Inspect paradigms and explain why Kalkoti meat lacks the low tone associated with some other aspirated Palula cognates.

analysis: Palula meec̣hí has final short-vowel accent, while Shina mac̣híi has final early-long ī accent. The shared final prominence contrasts with the old first-syllable long ā and implicates the i-bearing derivational formation rather than simple root accent preservation. Palula fronting is consistent with the i environment. Fly 9696 has a superficially similar modern outcome but an independently initial-accented old feminine, so the two histories must not be conflated.
unresolved: Identify the precise nominal suffix and its later reaccentuation/quantity history in each branch.

input: mātulá; mā́tulaka independently attested as an affectionate formation
analysis: Gilgit moól ‘uncle’ has late accent on a long contracted root, compatible with old final prominence after loss of the intervening and final syllabic material. The old first vowel was long but contraction of tu also matters, so this is less direct than bālá. The affectionate mā́tulaka provides a different old accent and formation, yet there is no independent reason to substitute it for the bare modern uncle noun.
unresolved: Read kinship inflection and acquire a tone-marked Kalkoti mool, whose HKAT citation alone is uninformative about tone.
